units.title: Fortran's History and Purpose
units.tip: Fortran is one of the oldest high-level programming languages, designed in the 1950s for scientific computing. It remains in widespread use today in numerical simulations, climate modeling, and engineering because it is extremely fast and optimized for mathematical operations.

lessons.title: What is Fortran and Where It's Used

exercises.question: What does FORTRAN originally stand for?
exercises.explain: FORTRAN was created to translate mathematical formulas into machine code. Its name reflects its original purpose: making it easy to write scientific computations.

exercises.question: In what decade was Fortran first developed?
exercises.explain: Fortran was created in the mid-1950s by IBM. It was one of the earliest high-level programming languages and is still used today.

exercises.question: Which field most heavily relies on Fortran today?
exercises.explain: Climate modeling, weather forecasting, quantum chemistry, and engineering simulations still rely on Fortran. It is optimized for numerical performance.

exercises.question: Why does Fortran remain popular for scientific computing?
exercises.answer: It produces fast code and optimizes mathematical operations efficiently
exercises.explain: Fortran compilers generate highly optimized machine code for numerical work. Its design is tightly focused on mathematical performance.
choices: It produces fast code and optimizes mathematical operations efficiently
It is the newest language available
It is the easiest to learn
It has the most libraries of any language

exercises.question: What type of problems did Fortran originally solve?
exercises.explain: Fortran was designed to help scientists and engineers write programs for calculations that would be tedious and error-prone by hand.

exercises.question: What is modern Fortran often called?
exercises.explain: Modern Fortran refers to versions from Fortran 90 onwards, which use free-form syntax (no fixed column rules) and include modules and advanced features.

exercises.question: What is a major difference between old and modern Fortran syntax?
exercises.answer: Old Fortran required fixed columns; modern Fortran is free-form
exercises.explain: Old Fortran (FORTRAN 77) used fixed columns: columns 1-5 for statement labels, column 6 for continuation marks, and columns 7-72 for code. Modern Fortran has no such restrictions.
choices: Old Fortran required fixed columns; modern Fortran is free-form

exercises.question: When was Fortran 90 released?
exercises.explain: Fortran 90 was a major revision released in 1991. It introduced modules, free-form syntax, and modern programming constructs.

exercises.question: What is a key feature added in Fortran 90?
exercises.explain: Fortran 90 introduced modules, which allow better code organization, encapsulation, and reusability. This was a major step toward modern programming practices.

exercises.question: Which Fortran revision added object-oriented features?
exercises.explain: Fortran 2003 added object-oriented features such as type extension and type-bound procedures. Fortran 90 added modules and free-form source, but not object orientation.

units.title: Program Structure and Syntax
units.tip: A Fortran program follows a clear structure: a program statement, variable declarations, executable statements, and an end statement. Modern free-form Fortran uses intuitive syntax similar to other languages, with no fixed column restrictions.

exercises.question: What keyword starts a Fortran program?
exercises.explain: A Fortran program begins with the program keyword, followed by a program name. Example: program hello_world

exercises.question: What statement marks the end of a Fortran program?
exercises.explain: Programs end with end program, optionally followed by the program name. This clearly marks the conclusion of the program.

exercises.question: What is the correct structure of a minimal Fortran program?
exercises.explain: A minimal program has a program statement, an end program statement, and executable statements in between. The name is optional in end program but good practice.

exercises.question: In free-form Fortran, where must statements appear?
exercises.answer: Anywhere on a line, with no column restrictions
exercises.explain: Free-form Fortran allows statements to start anywhere on a line. This is unlike old FORTRAN 77, which required specific column alignment.
choices: Only at the end of a line
Anywhere on a line, with no column restrictions
Only at the start of a line

exercises.question: How do you write a comment in modern Fortran?
exercises.explain: In modern Fortran, comments start with ! and continue to the end of the line. Example: ! This is a comment

exercises.question: What does 'implicit none' do?
exercises.answer: Requires all variables to be explicitly declared before use
exercises.explain: implicit none disables implicit typing, forcing you to declare every variable. This catches typos and makes code clearer. It is considered best practice.
choices: Requires all variables to be explicitly declared before use
Allows variables to be used without declaration
Removes all variable names from output

exercises.question: Where should 'implicit none' appear in a program?
exercises.answer: After the program statement, before variable declarations
exercises.explain: implicit none is placed right after the program statement (and any use statements), before you declare any variables. It applies to the whole program unit.
choices: After the program statement, before variable declarations
At the very end of the program
It can go anywhere in the program

exercises.question: What is the standard way to print output in Fortran?
exercises.answer: Use the print statement or write statement
exercises.explain: print * is the simplest form. write(*, *) is more flexible. Both send output to standard output.
choices: Use the print statement or write statement

exercises.question: What does 'print *' do in Fortran?
exercises.answer: Prints output to the screen with default formatting
exercises.explain: print * outputs variables or text to the screen. The asterisk means the format is chosen automatically by the compiler.
choices: Prints output to the screen with default formatting

exercises.question: What does the asterisk (*) represent in 'print *' and 'write(*, *)'?
exercises.explain: The first * means standard output (the screen). The second * means the format is list-directed (Fortran picks reasonable formatting).

units.title: Data Types and Declarations
units.tip: Fortran has five intrinsic (built-in) data types. The four you meet first are INTEGER for whole numbers, REAL for floating-point numbers, LOGICAL for true/false values, and CHARACTER for text (the fifth is COMPLEX). Each type serves a different purpose and affects how values are stored and computed.

exercises.question: What is the INTEGER type used for?
exercises.explain: INTEGER variables store whole numbers like -5, 0, 100. They cannot represent fractions or decimal values.

exercises.question: What is the REAL type used for?
exercises.explain: REAL variables store decimal numbers like 3.14, -2.5, or 0.001. They can represent fractions and are used for scientific calculations.

exercises.question: How do you declare an INTEGER variable in Fortran?
exercises.explain: The double colon :: separates the type from the variable name. Example: integer :: count

exercises.question: How do you declare a REAL variable in Fortran?
exercises.explain: Similar to INTEGER, REAL uses the double colon :: syntax. Example: real :: temperature

exercises.question: What is double precision in Fortran?
exercises.answer: A REAL type with more decimal places for higher accuracy
exercises.explain: double precision :: x declares a real variable with greater precision than a default REAL (usually twice the storage), useful for calculations needing high accuracy.
choices: A REAL type with more decimal places for higher accuracy
A variable that holds two numbers

exercises.question: What is the LOGICAL type used for?
exercises.explain: LOGICAL variables hold true or false values, useful for conditions and flags. Example: logical :: is_valid

exercises.question: How do you declare a LOGICAL variable?
exercises.explain: Use the same double colon syntax. Example: logical :: flag

exercises.question: What is the CHARACTER type used for?
exercises.explain: CHARACTER variables store text. Example: character(len=50) :: name stores a string up to 50 characters long.

exercises.question: How do you declare a CHARACTER variable with a specific length?
exercises.answer: character(len=N) :: variable_name, where N is the length
exercises.explain: The len parameter specifies how many characters the string can hold. Example: character(len=20) :: city
choices: character(len=N) :: variable_name, where N is the length

exercises.question: What does implicit typing mean in old Fortran?
exercises.answer: Variables starting with certain letters are automatically given a type
exercises.explain: Without implicit none, variables starting with I-N are INTEGER, and A-H, O-Z are REAL. This can cause bugs from typos, so implicit none is recommended.
choices: Variables starting with certain letters are automatically given a type

units.title: Control Flow and Loops
units.tip: Control flow statements direct the order in which code executes. DO loops repeat code, IF statements make decisions, and CASE statements handle multiple conditions. These are essential for writing realistic programs.

exercises.question: What is a DO loop used for?
exercises.answer: Repeating a block of code a fixed number of times
exercises.explain: DO loops iterate over a range of values. They are fundamental for processing arrays and performing repeated calculations.
choices: Repeating a block of code a fixed number of times

exercises.question: What is the syntax of a basic DO loop?
exercises.explain: This loop runs from i=1 to i=10. The variable i is the loop counter. End do marks the end of the loop.
choices: loop i from 1 to 10 ... end loop

exercises.question: What does 'do i = 1, n, 2' mean?
exercises.answer: Loop from 1 to n, incrementing i by 2 each iteration
exercises.explain: The third number is the step. This loop visits i=1, 3, 5, 7, ... up to n. Omitting the step defaults to 1.
choices: Loop from 1 to n, incrementing i by 2 each iteration
Loop from 1 to n and then repeat 2 times

exercises.question: How do you exit a DO loop early?
exercises.explain: exit immediately terminates the loop. You can use it inside an IF statement to break out when a condition is met.

exercises.question: What does the cycle statement do in a DO loop?
exercises.answer: Skips the rest of the current iteration and goes to the next one
exercises.explain: cycle is equivalent to continue in C. It jumps to the next iteration without executing remaining statements in the current iteration.
choices: Skips the rest of the current iteration and goes to the next one

exercises.question: What is an IF statement used for?
exercises.answer: Executing code only if a condition is true
exercises.explain: IF statements test a logical condition. If true, code inside executes. If false, it skips to else or end if.
choices: Executing code only if a condition is true

exercises.question: What is the syntax of an IF statement?
exercises.explain: The then keyword follows the condition. end if closes the statement. else is optional for handling the false case.

exercises.question: What are comparison operators in Fortran?
exercises.explain: These test equality (==), inequality (/=), and magnitudes. Note that /= means not equal in Fortran, unlike other languages.

exercises.question: What is a CASE statement used for?
exercises.answer: Handling multiple different values of a variable
exercises.explain: CASE is like switch in C. It tests one variable against many values and executes different code for each.
choices: Handling multiple different values of a variable
Looping a variable number of times

exercises.question: What is the syntax structure of a CASE statement?
exercises.explain: select case introduces the statement, case lists each condition, and end select closes it. Each case can handle one or multiple values.

units.title: Arrays and Array Operations
units.tip: Arrays store collections of values in a single variable. Fortran is built for array operations and can manipulate entire arrays with simple syntax. This makes it ideal for scientific computing with vectors and matrices.

exercises.question: How do you declare a 1D array in Fortran?
exercises.answer: integer :: arr(10) or integer, dimension(10) :: arr
exercises.explain: Both syntaxes create an array of 10 integers. The dimension is specified in parentheses.
choices: integer :: arr(10) or integer, dimension(10) :: arr

exercises.question: How do you declare a 2D array (matrix)?
exercises.answer: real :: matrix(3,4) or real, dimension(3,4) :: matrix
exercises.explain: This creates a 3x4 matrix (3 rows, 4 columns). Multiple dimensions are separated by commas.
choices: real :: matrix(3,4) or real, dimension(3,4) :: matrix

exercises.question: What is the default starting index for Fortran arrays?
exercises.explain: Fortran uses 1-based indexing by default, unlike C or Python which use 0-based indexing. The first element is arr(1), not arr(0).
choices: Always 0 for integer arrays and 1 for real arrays

exercises.question: How do you access the 5th element of an array?
exercises.explain: Array elements are accessed with parentheses. Example: x = arr(5) gets the 5th element.

exercises.question: How do you assign a value to an array element?
exercises.explain: Example: arr(3) = 42 sets the 3rd element to 42. This is standard assignment syntax.

exercises.question: What is array slicing in Fortran?
exercises.answer: Selecting a subset of elements from an array using a range
exercises.explain: arr(2:5) selects elements 2 through 5. arr(1:10:2) selects every 2nd element from 1 to 10.
choices: Selecting a subset of elements from an array using a range
Cutting an array into equal pieces

exercises.question: What does arr(2:5) mean?
exercises.explain: This is a slice that includes arr(2), arr(3), arr(4), and arr(5). The range is inclusive on both ends.
choices: The 2nd and 5th rows of a matrix

exercises.question: What is a key advantage of Fortran arrays?
exercises.answer: Operations can be applied to entire arrays at once without explicit loops
exercises.explain: Fortran supports array operations: arr1 + arr2 adds element-wise. This makes code concise and efficient for numerical computing.
choices: Operations can be applied to entire arrays at once without explicit loops
Arrays use less memory than scalars
Arrays can only hold whole numbers
Arrays can never be passed to procedures

exercises.question: How do you perform element-wise multiplication of two arrays in Fortran?
exercises.answer: c = a * b (if a and b are the same size)
exercises.explain: Fortran multiplies element-wise: c(i) = a(i) * b(i) for all i. This is an intrinsic array operation, no loop needed. matmul is matrix multiplication and dot_product returns a single number.
choices: c = a * b (if a and b are the same size)

exercises.question: What does the sum() function do on an array?
exercises.answer: Returns the sum of all array elements
exercises.explain: sum(arr) adds all elements: sum([1,2,3,4]) = 10. This is useful for totaling array values.
choices: Returns the sum of all array elements
Returns the product of all elements

units.title: Subroutines, Functions, and Modules
units.tip: Subroutines and functions break code into reusable pieces. Modules organize related code and data. These are essential for writing maintainable, large-scale programs in modern Fortran.

exercises.question: What is the difference between a subroutine and a function?
exercises.answer: Functions return a value; subroutines do not
exercises.explain: Functions compute and return a single value. Subroutines perform tasks but don't return a value (they modify arguments instead).
choices: Functions return a value; subroutines do not

exercises.question: What is the syntax to declare a function?
exercises.explain: The result clause names the variable that holds the returned value. Example: function add(x, y) result(total)

exercises.question: What is the syntax to declare a subroutine?
exercises.explain: A subroutine takes arguments but does not have a return type. Example: subroutine print_array(arr)

exercises.question: What does the 'return' statement do in a function or subroutine?
exercises.answer: Exits the procedure immediately and gives control back to the caller
exercises.explain: return leaves the procedure early and control goes back to the caller. A function's value is whatever its result variable holds at that point. It is optional at the end of a procedure.
choices: Exits the procedure immediately and gives control back to the caller

exercises.question: What does the 'call' statement do?
exercises.explain: call subroutine_name(arguments) executes the subroutine. Functions are invoked directly in expressions, not with call.

exercises.question: What is a module in Fortran?
exercises.answer: A container for related variables, functions, and subroutines
exercises.explain: Modules group related code and data. They provide encapsulation and make code reusable. A module can be used by multiple programs.
choices: A container for related variables, functions, and subroutines

exercises.question: What is the syntax to declare a module?
exercises.explain: A module starts with the module keyword and ends with end module. Example: module math_utils ... end module

exercises.question: How do you use code from a module in a program?
exercises.explain: use module_name imports everything from the module. Example: use math_utils makes all functions and variables in math_utils available.

exercises.question: What is the 'contains' keyword used for in a module?
exercises.answer: Marks the start of the subroutines and functions section
exercises.explain: contains separates the declarations section from the procedures (subroutines and functions). It marks where the code implementations begin.
choices: Marks the start of the subroutines and functions section

exercises.question: What is the benefit of using modules?
exercises.explain: Modules let you group related functionality, reuse code across programs, and hide internal details. This makes large projects more manageable.
choices: They are required for all programs
